item.description: arXiv:2611.04730v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with integer coefficients of absolute value less than $2^b$. Using Pan's approximate factorization theorem, we give a deterministic algorithm that finds all distinct integer roots of $f$ in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations. This matches the bit size of the input up to logarithmic factors and does not require $f$ to be square-free. Since we were unable to verify parts of the running time analysis of Pan's theorem, we also give a self-contained deterministic algorithm with running time $\widetilde O(nb+\min(n,b)^3b^2)$, which is $\widetilde O(nb)$ whenever $b\leq n^{1/4}$. This answers a question of Harvey and Hittmeir (2022), who asked whether integer roots can be found deterministically in quasilinear time, conditionally on Pan's theorem, and unconditionally for $b\leq n^{1/4}$. The fastest previous deterministic algorithm, due to Nir, takes $\widetilde O(n^{3/2}b)$ bit operations and works only for square-free polynomials. Instead of $p$-adic lifting, we combine approximate complex root finding with exact polynomial evaluation. We first approximate the complex roots of the polynomial formed by the top $\min(n,b)+1$ coefficients of $f$. Every integer root $r$ of $f$ with $|r|\geq 2$ lies within distance $2$ of some complex root of this truncated polynomial. Rounding the real parts of the approximate roots therefore gives a list of $O(\min(n,b))$ candidate integers that is guaranteed to contain all integer roots of $f$. Although a single candidate can have up to $b$ bits, a bound via the Mahler measure shows that the bit lengths of all candidates sum to $O(b)$. This allows us to test all candidates by exact multipoint evaluation in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations.
item.dc:creator: Yansong Feng, Itamar Nir

item.title: Geometric Bin Packing Beyond Convexity: Approximation Schemes without Augmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.04829v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the geometric bin packing problem for simple polygonal regions, i.e., non-degenerate, connected, rational regions, in the minimum number of unit-square bins, allowing only translations. We even consider packing general non-convex objects, possibly with holes, where we can then pack smaller objects. Previous schemes cover squares (MOR'06), circles and other $L_p$-balls (Algorithmica'16), sufficiently skewed rectangles (Algorithmica'23), and convex fat objects with a constant number of distinct shapes under resource augmentation (arXiv'24, WAOA'23). The result for circles and other $L_p$-balls needs bin augmentation to obtain rational packing realizations. For restricted classes of $L$-shaped polygons, Gerlach et al. (SoCG'26) give constant worst-case guarantees, while for general non-convex objects, bounding-box reductions give just approximation factors that depend on fatness. Against this background, we present a general framework that provides asymptotic polynomial-time approximation schemes (APTAS) for bin packing of any fixed class of simple polygonal regions satisfying just two assumptions. First, covering any object by the grid cells intersecting its interior in any sufficiently fine square grid, relative to the object's bounding box, increases its area by at most a small fraction. Second, the class can be partitioned into a constant number of sequences such that each object in a sequence can be translated to fit inside every preceding object. In particular, certain classes of star-shaped polygons and more general polygonal regions, including some with simple holes, satisfy both assumptions. In addition, our framework does not require a bound on the objects' boundary complexity. We emphasize that our results require no bin augmentation whatsoever and yield explicit, exact rational packings of polynomial encoding length for all input objects.
item.dc:creator: Lucas de Oliveira Silva, Elisa Dell'Arriva, Fl\'avio Keidi Miyazawa

item.title: Best-of-Many-Worlds MMS Allocation for Chores with Sublinear Disposals
item.description: arXiv:2611.04884v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study randomized allocations (lotteries) of indivisible chores under additive costs and introduce the notion of MMS1, which requires each agent's bundle to satisfy the maximin share (MMS) bound after the removal of at most one chore. Our main result establishes that every instance admits an ex-ante proportional lottery in whose support every allocation is MMS1 and all but $o(n)$ agents satisfy MMS. Consequently, every realized allocation can be made MMS by disposing of at most $o(n)$ chores. The proposed framework further achieves ex-ante proportionality alongside ex-post $4/3$-MMS, $o(n)$-AMMS, or $1$-out-of-$d$ MMS for $d=(1-o(1))n$. These guarantees substantially improve upon state-of-the-art bounds for MMS allocation for chores with disposal or subsidy, best-of-both-worlds fairness, approximate AMMS, and ordinal MMS approximations.
item.dc:creator: Zehan Lin, Xiaowei Wu, Shengwei Zhou

item.title: Local Distributed Computation under Crash Failures
item.description: arXiv:2611.04898v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study deterministic algorithms for locally checkable graph problems in the synchronous LOCAL model with crash failures, where a crashing node may send messages to only some neighbors. We introduce consistent neighborhoods: partial radius-$R$ views that agree locally across surviving edges and are complete without crashes. For $R=T+\ell+1$, these views allow local simulation of $T$-round fault-free algorithms that remain correct on subgraphs, satisfying constraints wherever the radius-$\ell$ checking neighborhood contains no crash. On graphs with at most $n$ nodes and maximum degree at most $\Delta\geq3$, we construct these views in $O(\min\{n,(\Delta-1)^R,R\Delta f\})$ rounds when a crash bound $f\geq1$ is globally known; the first two bounds require no knowledge of $f$. For $\Delta=2$ or girth greater than $2R$, including forests, $O(R)$ rounds suffice. Our upper bounds are essentially tight in suitable parameter regimes. One crash can force $\Omega(n)$ rounds even for $R=3$ on diameter-two graphs. For each fixed $\Delta\geq3$ and sufficiently large $R$, we prove a $(\Delta-1)^{R-O(\sqrt R)}$ lower bound even with crashes restricted to round beginnings. We also prove an $\Omega(\Delta Rf)$ lower bound when $R\geq4\lceil\log_{\Delta-1}f\rceil+4$ and $n\geq\Delta Rf$. For locally checkable labeling (LCL) problems, we preserve $O(\log^* n)$ complexity under any number of crashes whenever this bound holds without faults on all graphs with a fixed degree bound. In contrast, we construct an LCL on graphs of maximum degree at most five with fault-free complexity $\Theta(\log n)$ and crash-tolerant complexity $\Theta(n)$. Finally, any fault-free sinkless-orientation algorithm can be transformed to tolerate any number of crashes with only one additional round, guaranteeing correctness even at surviving nodes adjacent to crashes.
item.dc:creator: Diana Ghinea, Fabian Kuhn, Chen-Da Liu-Zhang, Zahra Parsaeian

item.title: A Low-Diameter Nash-Williams--Tutte Theorem
item.description: arXiv:2611.05043v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Nash-Williams--Tutte theorem characterizes the existence of $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees by a condition on every vertex partition. We prove that, for simple graphs, the same condition guarantees $k$ edge-disjoint spanning trees, each of diameter $O(n/\delta)$ and with $O((n/\delta)\log(\delta+1))$ internal vertices, where $n$ is the number of vertices and $\delta$ is the minimum degree. Both bounds hold simultaneously for every tree, with absolute implicit constants independent of $k$, and each is asymptotically optimal in general. Our proof is constructive and yields a randomized algorithm with expected running time $\tilde{O}(n^5)$. We derive applications to short edge-disjoint routes and weak linkages, small Steiner trees, and survivable networks with short paths. The joint bounds also yield low-diameter spanning Eulerian subgraphs and short tours for postman and general routing problems.
item.dc:creator: Pin-Hsian Lee, Peng-Ting Lin, Meng-Tsung Tsai, Ting-An Wu

item.title: Beyond Multi-Index Models: Learning Intersections of Degree-2 PTFs
item.description: arXiv:2611.05114v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give an algorithm for PAC learning intersections of $k$ degree-2 polynomial threshold functions over $R^d$ under a Gaussian distribution. Our algorithm achieves classification error $\epsilon$ using $d^{O(k)}2^{O_k(\log^3(1/\epsilon))}$ time and samples, improving over the $d^{O(k^2/\epsilon^2)}$ running time of the polynomial regression approach. To our knowledge, our result is the first to obtain a dimension exponent independent of the accuracy parameter, even for $k=2$. We complement our algorithmic result with an SQ lower bound showing that the complexity dependence of $d^{\Omega(k)}$ is unavoidable. Lifting the input to polynomial features turns the target into an intersection of $k$ halfspaces. This suggests using the first two labeled moments for subspace recovery. In the lifted space, however, these moments can reveal nothing. Our starting point is a Gaussian comparison theorem showing that, for sufficiently regular defining quadratics, the labeled moments needed for subspace recovery are approximately preserved. To handle arbitrary defining quadratics, we establish a new structural result showing that every direction with significant resampling influence can be detected through degree-$O(k)$ moments. These results yield an initial $d^{O(k)}2^{\mathrm{poly}_k(1/\epsilon)}$-time learner using adaptive restrictions. To improve the exponential dependence on $1/\epsilon$, we develop a two-stage dimension-reduction approach that avoids the costly adaptive partitioning. After identifying a subspace containing all directions with large influence, we use generalized regularity and Gaussian comparison to recover the remaining relevant quadratic features through a new derivative-based moment operator. The recovered features support an intersection close to the target. Combining them with robust hinge-loss minimization gives our quasipolynomial-time learner.
item.dc:creator: Ilias Diakonikolas, Daniel M. Kane, Mingchen Ma, Lisheng Ren, Trung Tran

item.title: Quantum Query Lower Bounds from Classical Moment Matching
item.description: arXiv:2611.05117v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We prove a quantum analogue of the classical moment matching method, a popular framework used to prove lower bounds in property testing. For two random variables $X_0$ and $X_1$ whose moments match up to the first $r-1$ moments, the classical moment matching method says that no classical algorithm can reliably distinguish between input instances of length $N$ constructed from $X_0$ and $X_1$, respectively, unless it performs at least $\Omega(N^{1-1/r})$ queries. While this method has been widely explored since its inception in the seminal work of Raskhodnikova, Ron, Shpilka, and Smith (STOC 2007) to prove lower bounds for symmetric properties, it has remained an open question whether a quantum analogue of it could be proved. We prove two variants of this quantum moment matching method, which are incomparable. Our first quantum query lower bound scales as $\Omega(N^{1/2-1/(2r)})$, while our second moment matching theorem yields a sharper lower bound of $\Omega(N^{1/2-1/(2(2^r-1))})$, albeit for smaller parameter ranges. Our results combine a new continuous hybrid argument with the polynomial method. The continuous hybrid argument compares two hard input distributions generated from i.i.d. samples by continuously varying both distributions, keeping them identically distributed at every intermediate stage. It reduces the comparison to the effect of changing the distribution of a single sample. The polynomial method then cancels the terms determined by the matched moments. We apply these moment matching theorems to prove new optimal lower bounds on $k$-distinctness, $k$-star-freeness, planarity and outerplanarity testing, as well as to improve prior lower bounds on image size testing and $K$-junta testing by logarithmic factors. A key advantage of our framework is its simplicity: it reduces quantum lower bound proofs to the construction of suitable moment-matching distributions.
item.dc:creator: Chandrima Kayal, Fr\'ed\'eric Magniez, Sayantan Sen, D\'aniel Szab\'o

item.title: Efficient Equilibrium Computation in Colonel Blotto Games
item.description: arXiv:2611.05221v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Colonel Blotto is a fundamental resource-allocation game in which two players divide their budgets across battlefields, and the higher allocation on each battlefield wins its value. The problem of computing an equilibrium efficiently has remained unresolved for its classical continuous version with arbitrary budgets and with values that may vary across battlefields but are the same for both players. We give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme that computes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$, and nearly linear in the input length for fixed $\varepsilon$. For sufficiently balanced budgets and battlefield values, we also compute exact equilibria in linear time.
item.dc:creator: Martin Bichler, Abheek Ghosh

item.title: Agnostic Learning by Imitating
item.description: arXiv:2611.05346v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given a class of machine learning models and sample access to a data distribution with binary labels, which computational task is harder: training a discriminative model that distinguishes positive and negative labels as well as the best member of the class, or training a generative model whose outputs are indistinguishable from real data by all members of the class? We prove that these two fundamental tasks in computational learning theory are not just closely related, but actually equivalent to each other in complexity. One direction of this equivalence was previously known. Indeed, the powerful regularity lemma in complexity theory gives an efficient oracle reduction from the indistinguishability task (a.k.a. multiaccuracy) to the distinguishing task (a.k.a. agnostic learning) in the style of boosting algorithms. Our main contribution is an efficient oracle reduction in the other direction. Taking this idea further, we show that a multiaccuracy oracle is a remarkably powerful primitive, achieving not just agnostic learning but also a wide range of seemingly more demanding learning objectives via similarly efficient and direct constructions. Our results crucially use the power of making adaptive queries to the oracle, and stand in stark contrast to prior work, which showed that post-processing a single multiaccurate predictor is insufficient for even weak forms of learning. On a technical level, we draw a connection between our (offline) problem and a version of no-regret learning in the online setting, which allows us to use follow-the-leader type algorithms to modify the label distribution and aggregate the predictions of the multiaccuracy oracle.
item.dc:creator: S\'ilvia Casacuberta, Parikshit Gopalan, Varun Kanade, Omer Reingold, Konstantinos Stavropoulos, Pranay Tankala

item.title: Breaking the quantum barriers for Graph Collision
item.description: arXiv:2611.05356v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the graph collision problem, the task is to decide whether a known graph on $n$ vertices contains an edge with both endpoints marked, given query access to the input bits specifying the marked vertices. We first refute the conjectured $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ query lower bound with a bounded error quantum algorithm using $\widetilde O(n^{92/139})$ queries. We then refine this approach to obtain a $\widetilde O(n^{11/17})$ query algorithm. We also obtain a $\widetilde O((nq)^{11/17})$ query bound for all (partial) Boolean output functions with positive certificate complexity at most 2 and alphabet size $q$, contrasting a known $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ lower bound for such problems with large alphabet sizes. We complement these algorithms with an $\Omega(\sqrt{n\log n})$ quantum query lower bound for graph collision, exceeding the $O(\sqrt n)$ certificate complexity barrier for the positive adversary method.
item.dc:creator: Arjan Cornelissen, Amin Shiraz Gilani, Shiva Kintali, Fran\c{c}ois Le Gall, Subhasree Patro, Xingyu Zhou

item.title: Loop unrolling of UCA models: distance labeling
item.description: arXiv:2202.10527v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A proper circular-arc (PCA) model is a pair $M = (C, A)$ where $C$ is a circle and $A$ is a family of inclusion-free arcs on $C$ whose extremes are pairwise different. The model $M$ represents a digraph $D$ that has one vertex $v(a)$ for each $a \in A$ and one edge $v(a) \to v(b)$ for each pair of arcs $a,b \in A(M)$ such that the beginning point of $b$ belongs to $a$. For $k \geq 0$, the $k$-th power $D^k$ of $D$ has the same vertices as $D$ and $v(a) \to v(b)$ is an edge of $D^k$ when $a\neq b$ and the distance from $v(a)$ to $v(b)$ in $D$ is at most $k$. A unit circular-arc (UCA) model is a PCA model $U = (C,A)$ in which all the arcs have the same length $\ell+1$. If $\ell$, the length $c$ of $C$, and the extremes of the arcs of $A$ are integer, then $U$ is a $(c,\ell)$-CA model. For $i \geq 0$, the model $i \times U$ of $U$ is obtained by replacing each arc $(s,s+\ell+1)$ with the arc $(s,s+i\ell+1)$. If $U$ represents a digraph $D$, then $U$ is $k$-multiplicative when $i \times U$ represents $D^i$ for every $0 \leq i \leq k$. In this article we design a linear time algorithm to decide if a PCA model $M$ is equivalent to a $k$-multiplicative UCA model when $k$ is given as input. The algorithm either outputs a $k$-multiplicative UCA model $U$ equivalent to $M$ or a negative certificate that can be authenticated in linear time. Our main technical tool is a new characterization of those PCA models that are equivalent to $k$-multiplicative UCA models. For $k=1$, this characterization yields a new algorithm for the classical representation problem that is simpler than the previously known algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Francisco J Soulignac, Pablo Terlisky

item.title: Variable Parameter Analysis for Scheduling One Machine
item.description:
arXiv:2211.02107v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In contrast to the fixed parameter analysis (FPA), in the variable parameter analysis (VPA) the value of the target problem parameter is not fixed, it rather depends on the structure of a given problem instance and tends to have a favorable asymptotic behavior when the size of the input increases. While applying the VPA to an intractable optimization problem with $n$ objects, the exponential-time dependence in enumeration of the feasible solution set is attributed solely to the variable parameter $
u$, $
u<<n$. As opposed to the FPA, the VPA does not imply any restriction on some problem parameters, it rather takes an advantage of a favorable nature of the problem, which permits to reduce the cost of enumeration of the solution space. Our main technical contribution is a variable parameter algorithm for a strongly $\mathsf{NP}$-hard single-machine scheduling problem to minimize maximum job lateness. The target variable parameter $
u$ is the number of jobs with some specific characteristics, the ``emerging'' ones. The solution process is separated in two phases. At phase 1 a partial solution including $n-
u$ non-emerging jobs is constructed in a low degree polynomial time. At phase 2 less than $
u!$ permutations of the $
u$ emerging jobs are considered. Each of them are incorporated into the partial schedule of phase 1. Doe to the results of an earlier conducted experimental study, $
u/n$ varied from $1/4$ for small problem instances to $1/10$ for the largest tested problem instances, so that that the ratio becomes closer to 0 for large $n$s.
item.dc:creator: Nodari Vakhania

item.title: Improved Algorithms for Unrelated Crowd Worker Scheduling in Mobile Social Networks
item.description: arXiv:2603.26129v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies task scheduling with unrelated crowd workers in mobile social networks, where the service time of a task depends on the crowd worker that performs it, and the objective is to minimize the total weighted completion time. For identical crowd workers, we tighten the approximation ratio of the Largest-Ratio-First (LRF) algorithm and update the competitive ratio of its online version. For unrelated crowd workers, we show that the time-indexed rounding framework of Im and Li remains valid when worker-dependent contact delays are added, which yields a randomized algorithm with an expected approximation ratio of 1.45; this improves upon the expected ratio of $1.5+\epsilon$ obtained in our previous work for identical crowd workers. We also derandomize this algorithm. To improve computational efficiency, we further propose an algorithm that exploits the optimality of the Smith-ratio order on a single crowd worker, and we prove that it is a deterministic 1.5-approximation algorithm and that its polynomial-time version achieves an approximation ratio arbitrarily close to 1.5. Experiments on synthetic instances and on instances derived from real contact traces show that this algorithm outperforms three variants of LRF in all tested settings, with the largest advantage when the crowd workers are highly heterogeneous, performs on par with a local-search heuristic for unrelated machines, and is within 0.4\% of the optimum on average on small instances that can be solved exactly.
item.dc:creator: Chi-Yeh Chen

item.title: Fully Scalable MPC Algorithms for Euclidean Clustering: Constant Approximation in Constant Rounds
item.description: arXiv:2604.00954v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study Euclidean $k$-Means and $k$-Median under the Massively Parallel Computation (MPC) model, focusing on the \emph{fully scalable} setting. Previously, fully scalable algorithms for $k$-Means and/or $k$-Median either required $O(\log\log n\cdot\log\log\log n)$ rounds [Cohen-Addad, Kuhn, and Parsaeian; SODA'26] or guaranteed only an $O(\log n)$-approximation [Goranci, Jiang, Kiss, Kong, Qian, and Szilagyi; SODA'26]. In this paper, we close this gap by giving the first fully scalable algorithms for both problems, which work even when $k$ is polynomially larger than the local memory, and \emph{simultaneously} achieve an $O(1)$-approximation and $O(1)$ round complexity. Technically, we devise a new variant of the MP algorithm [Mettu and Plaxton, SICOMP'03] that computes a \emph{fractional solution satisfying the Lagrangian Multiplier Preserving (LMP) property}. Importantly, this LMP guarantee holds even under arbitrary distance distortions, a feature that is crucial for efficient MPC implementations. We then give a novel MPC rounding algorithm that first rounds to a bicriteria solution with $k+O(n^{1-\epsilon})$ centers and then uses an \emph{iterative kernelization} idea to convert it into one with exactly $k$ centers.
item.dc:creator: Artur Czumaj, Shaofeng H. -C. Jiang, Yaonan Jin, Jianing Lou, Weicheng Wang

item.title: Scalable Exact Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering via Sparse Geographic Distance Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2604.11656v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Exact hierarchical agglomerative clustering (HAC) of large spatial datasets is limited in practice by the $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ time and memory required for the full pairwise distance matrix. We present GSHAC (Geographically Sparse Hierarchical Agglomerative Clustering), a system that makes exact HAC feasible at scales of millions of geographic features on a commodity workstation. GSHAC replaces the distance matrix with a sparse geographic distance graph containing only pairs within a user-specified geodesic bound $h_{\max}$, constructed in $\mathcal{O}(n \cdot k)$ time via spatial indexing, where $k$ is the mean number of neighbors within $h_{\max}$. Connected components of this graph define independent subproblems, and we prove that the resulting assignments are exact for all standard linkage methods at any cut height $h \le h_{\max}$. For single linkage, an MST-based path keeps memory at $\mathcal{O}(n_k + m_k)$ per component. Applied to a global mining inventory ($n = 261{,}073$), the system completes in 12 s (109 MiB peak HAC memory) versus $\approx 545$ GiB for the dense baseline. On a 2-million-point GeoNames sample, all tested thresholds completed in under 3 minutes with peak memory under 3 GiB. We provide a scikit-learn-compatible implementation for direct integration into GIS workflows.
item.dc:creator: Victor Maus, Vinicius Pozzobon Borin

item.title: Optimal Zonotope Containment via Adaptive Gaussian Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2605.04183v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the convex-body containment problem $\max\{s >0 : s Z \subseteq Q\}$, where the outer body $Q \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is described by a membership oracle and the inner body $Z \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is a zonotope. Our main result is a sampling-based $O(\sqrt{d/\log d})$-approximation algorithm for this problem that matches the lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{d/\log d})$ by Khot and Naor in the oracle model. Starting from approximate Lewis position, the algorithm samples Gaussian directions and adaptively shortens and repositions the generators. Its analysis combines preservation of the support in a fixed direction with contraction of the corresponding functional after renormalization. Crucially, the algorithm works directly with the input generators and does not use zonotope sparsification. We complement this result with a \emph{universal} $\Omega(\sqrt{d/\log d})$ lower bound holding for \emph{all} full-dimensional zonotopes when the number of oracle queries is polynomial in $d$. Finally, we consider containment problems $\max\{s >0 : s K \subseteq Q\}$, for general convex bodies $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$. A result of Nasz{\'o}di on approximating $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ by a polytope implies a $\Theta(d/\log d)$ approximation algorithm in polynomial time when the centroid of $K$ is the origin. We show the tightness of this approximation factor in the oracle model via a reduction to the circumradius computation. Our lower bound holds for centrally symmetric convex sets, implying that Barvinok's optimal $O(\sqrt{d})$-approximation of a centrally symmetric convex body by a polytope with a polynomial number of vertices cannot be computed in polynomial time.
item.dc:creator: Friedrich Eisenbrand, Thomas Rothvoss, Matteo Russo, Ruben Skorupinski

item.title: Nearly Optimal Submodular Sparsification, with and without Cardinality Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2606.20777v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the sparsification of decomposable submodular functions: given a sum $F(S) = \sum_{i=1}^m f_i(S)$ of $m$ nonnegative submodular functions on an $n$-element ground set $[n]$ (without assuming monotonicity or symmetry), the goal is to find a sparse reweighting $\widetilde{F}(S) = \sum_{i=1}^m w_i f_i(S)$ with at most $s \ll m$ nonzero weights that preserves $F(S)$ within a $(1 \pm \varepsilon)$ factor across a target family of queries. For all subset queries $S \subseteq [n]$, we give a polynomial-time randomized algorithm that constructs a sparsifier of size $O(n^2 \log n / \varepsilon^2)$. This improves upon the previous best upper bound of $O(n^3 / \varepsilon^2)$ by Kenneth and Krauthgamer and resolves their open conjecture up to a logarithmic factor, matching the $\Omega(n^2)$ lower bound from directed cuts. Motivated by capacity budgets in submodular applications and the Restricted Isometry Property (RIP) in compressed sensing, we further study submodular sparsification under a cardinality constraint $|S| \le k$, and obtain a polynomial-time algorithm that constructs a sparsifier of size $O(n k \log n / \varepsilon^2)$, nearly matching the $\Omega(nk)$ lower bound. This shows that a cardinality constraint unconditionally reduces the size of general submodular sparsifiers by a factor of roughly $k/n$; we complement this with $\Omega(n)$ lower bounds showing that even regular symmetric or almost-regular monotone submodular functions cannot be sparsified to $o(n)$ size for $k = 2$ and $k = 1$, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Zhengting Bao, Dongrun Cai, Xue Chen, Yuchen He, Chihao Zhang

item.title: Tight Bounds for $(1+\epsilon)$-Approximation for Minimum Spanning Trees in Doubling Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2607.13284v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The minimum spanning tree (MST) problem is one of the most basic optimization problems on metric spaces and graphs. We study the problem of computing a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation to the MST of an $n$-point metric space of doubling dimension $\mathrm{ddim}$. In doubling metrics, previous deterministic algorithms incur a running time with dependence $\epsilon^{-O(\mathrm{ddim})}$. We give a deterministic algorithm that computes a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate MST in time $$ O_{\mathrm{ddim}}\left(n\log n+ \min\left\{n^2,\frac{n}{\epsilon}\log(1/\epsilon)\right\}\right) $$ in the standard real RAM model with a unit-cost exact-distance oracle. For bounded doubling dimension, this improves the previous dependence on $\epsilon$ to essentially linear in $\epsilon^{-1}$. We complement this algorithm with a lower bound of $$ \Omega \!\left(n\log n+ \min\left\{n^2,\frac{n}{\epsilon}\log(1/\epsilon)\right\}\right) $$ on running time in the same model, already for metrics of doubling dimension at most seven, showing that our running time is essentially tight. For points in $\mathbb R^d$ with $d = O(1)$, exploiting Euclidean geometry allows us to further improve the dependence on $\epsilon$. We obtain a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate MST in expected time $$ O_d\left( n \log n + \min\left\{n^2, \frac{n}{\epsilon^{1 - \beta_d}} \log^{1-\beta_d}(1/\epsilon) \right\} \right) $$ for some $\beta_d=\Theta(1/d)$, improving the accuracy-dependent term $n\epsilon^{-2}\log^2(1/\epsilon)$ of Arya and Mount [SODA'16].
item.dc:creator: Jan H\"ockendorff, Felix Hommelsheim, Christian Sohler, Di Yue

item.title: Approximate Dual Separation for the Cluster LP: a 1.387-approximation for Correlation Clustering
item.description: arXiv:2607.27829v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a $(1.3865+\epsilon)$-approximation for correlation clustering on complete graphs, improving the previous best factor of $1.485+\epsilon$ of Cao et al. (STOC'24). Our first main contribution is an efficient weak separation oracle for the cluster-LP dual. Given signed vertex weights $q$, it either finds a set $S$ with $q(S)>cost(S)$ or certifies that $q/(1+\epsilon)$ is dual feasible, where $cost(S)$ measures the correlation clustering disagreements attributed to $S$ in any clustering in which $S$ is a cluster. Via the ellipsoid method, this yields $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate primal and dual solutions for the fractional cluster LP in deterministic time $2^{poly(1/\epsilon)}n^{O(1)}$ . The separator works directly on the original instance, without global preclustering: a novel localization argument restricts the search to a small universe, where weak regularity handles the resulting dense quadratic minimization. Complementing this result, we prove that exact dual separation and cluster-LP optimization are NP-hard, even for complete unweighted instances. Our second main contribution is a new rounding of the cluster LP. It combines cluster-based rounding with a continuous conditional pivot rule, and its analysis relies on single variance inequality with explicit weights. This bounds the cluster-LP integrality gap by $1.3865$, near its known lower bound of $4/3$, and gives a per-instance primal--dual certificate of approximation. Finally, we extend our separator to obtain a $(1.92+\epsilon)$-approximation for seeded correlation clustering (where each cluster may contain at most one seed from a prescribed seed set), and to bounded-weight instances, yielding a deterministic polynomial-time approximate implementation of the cluster-insertion primitive used in combinatorial correlation clustering.
item.dc:creator: David Garc\'ia-Soriano, Antoine Schohn

item.title: Dense Language Generation Made Simple: Deterministic, Randomized, and Multi-Order Algorithms
item.description: arXiv:2608.01320v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language generation in the limit is a theoretical framework for studying how a generator can learn to produce new valid strings from a stream of positive examples. In this model, an adversary chooses an unknown language from a countable family and enumerates its elements in an arbitrary order, while the generator must eventually output only elements of the language that have not yet appeared in the enumeration. Reliable generation is thus formalized through two eventual guarantees: validity and novelty relative to the observed data. To further quantify the breadth of the generator's outputs, Kleinberg and Wei (FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) introduced lower density as a measure of output coverage. Given an order representing the importance or relevance of possible outputs, lower density is the asymptotic lower bound, as $n$ grows, on the fraction of the first $n$ elements of the target language that the generator outputs before they appear in the data. Kleinberg and Wei showed that $1/2$ is the optimal lower-density guarantee for deterministic algorithms. We develop a simple and unified framework for obtaining optimal lower-density guarantees. We first give a deterministic algorithm that recovers the optimal guarantee of $1/2$ with a significantly simpler analysis than prior work. We then demonstrate the flexibility of our framework through two extensions. First, against an oblivious adversary, randomization raises the optimal guarantee to $1-1/e$. Second, for any finite collection of orders, the optimal deterministic and randomized guarantees can be achieved simultaneously with respect to every order, so accommodating multiple notions of importance or relevance entails no loss in the optimal guarantee.
item.dc:creator: Ziyi Cai, Shuangping Li, Yiheng Shen, Kangning Wang, Peng Zhang

item.title: Concentration from Product Moments via an Additional Element of Randomness
item.description: arXiv:2608.04125v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The standard method of exponential moments for proving concentration bounds can often be replaced by an argument based on elementary symmetric polynomials. We introduce an additional element of randomness into this framework, which reduces the problem to bounding product moments over a uniformly sampled set of indices. We show that this approach gives useful bounds in three settings. For read-$\Delta$ families under limited independence, we obtain bounds governed by the degrees of randomly induced dependency subgraphs, improving the dependence on worst-case degrees. For random linear hashing over arbitrary finite fields with (semi-)random inputs, we derive fixed-bin and maximum-load bounds by controlling the rank defect of random tuples of input keys. Finally, for stochastic processes, we show how decay of product moments yields concentration bounds, recovering the spectral and mixing-time scales for finite-state Markov chains.
item.dc:creator: Michael Saks, Aravind Srinivasan, Renata Valieva

item.title: Counting Linear Extensions Faster than $2^n$
item.description: arXiv:2608.19505v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic algorithm that counts the linear extensions of any $n$-element poset in $O^*(33^{n/6}) \le O^*(1.791^n)$ time and space, breaking the $O^*(2^n)$ barrier of standard order-ideal dynamic programming without assumptions on height, width, or dimension. Our algorithm fixes an antichain $B$ and tracks order ideals only on the remaining core $V \setminus B$. For each element $v \in B$ that has successors in the core, we guess which of those successors appears first in the linear extension, reducing all upper constraints on $v$ to a single deadline. An element $v \in B$ becomes available once all of its core predecessors have been placed; available elements with the same deadline then face identical remaining constraints, so the dynamic program only needs to record how many available elements have each deadline and weight transitions by the number of choices for the next element. Taking $B$ to be a maximum antichain and balancing this dynamic program against a Dilworth chain partition yields an $O^*(1.89^n)$ algorithm. To obtain our main bound, we use a minimum-cut computation in an auxiliary bipartite network to find an antichain $B$ whose comparability neighborhood $R$ satisfies $|B| \ge 5|R|$ while the remainder $V \setminus (B \cup R)$ partitions into stars with at most five leaves. Since a $j$-leaf star has $2^j+1$ independent sets and $(2^j+1)^{1/(j+1)} \le 33^{1/6}$ for $1 \le j \le 5$, combining the star bound on the remainder with our state bound on $B \cup R$ gives $O^*(33^{n/6})$ time and space.
item.dc:creator: Keigo Oka

item.title: Recovery Beats Storage: Improved Space for Preprocessed 3SUM
item.description: arXiv:2608.22355v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The 3SUM problem asks, given sets $A,B,C$ of integers, whether there exist $a\in A$ and $b\in B$ whose sum belongs to $C$. In the preprocessed variant with unknown $C$, one preprocesses sets $A$ and $B$, each of size $n$, and subsequently answers a query specified by subsets $A'\subseteq A$, $B'\subseteq B$ and a target set $C'$ of size $O(n)$, by solving the 3SUM instance $(A',B',C')$. Kirkpatrick, Kuszmaul, Mathialagan, and Vassilevska Williams [ICALP 2026] gave the first algorithm with subquadratic space for this problem, achieving $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2+\epsilon})$ query time using $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-2\epsilon/3})$ space, for every $\epsilon\in[0,1/2]$. Their algorithm employs separate mechanisms for heavy and light targets, and for each heavy target it stores explicitly the list of pairs $(a,b)$ whose sum is congruent to it modulo a random prime $p$ but differs from it. These lists dominate the space bound. We present a unified construction that uses a single mechanism for all queries. Instead of storing these lists of pairs, our algorithm recovers on demand the residue class of the target modulo a random prime by inverting the function $(a,b)\mapsto (a+b\bmod p)$. Additionally, instead of storing the heavy targets, it recomputes at query time a set that covers them. This leads to an improved space bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{2-\epsilon})$, while maintaining the same query time. Moreover, our construction is the first to achieve subquadratic space while supporting adaptively chosen queries.
item.dc:creator: Amir Carmel, Yakov Kosoburd, Robert Krauthgamer

item.title: A Spectral Local-to-Global Principle for Spin Systems on Graphs with Girth At Least Five
item.description: arXiv:2608.25491v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is proved that, for every $\delta \in (0,1)$, the Glauber dynamics for the uniform distribution on proper $q$-colorings is rapidly mixing when $q \geq (1+\delta)\Delta$ and the underlying graph has girth at least $5$ and maximum degree $\Delta = \Omega_\delta(1)$. This result also extends to general multi-spin systems satisfying a $\textit{local spectral contraction}$ condition, including the anti-ferromagnetic Potts model with $q\geq (1+\delta)(1-\beta)\Delta$. These results are achieved by a new spectral local-to-global principle on graphs with girth at least five for general multi-spin systems, and a novel Fourier analysis for Glauber dynamics on a star. The main ideas behind all the proofs were developed through several rounds of interaction with GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Chen, Kuikui Liu

item.title: On the Instance Optimality of Bidirectional Dijkstra's Algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2608.26952v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study instance optimality for the shortest $st$-path problem on positive-weight graphs, emphasizing how graph structure and query access determine the cost of certifying shortest paths. For undirected simple graphs in the standard adjacency-list model, we prove instance-sensitive lower bounds against all randomized algorithms that are correct on every admissible input. A quantitative reservoir argument bounds the instance-optimality ratio of corrected bidirectional Dijkstra in terms of its exploration size and the vertex count. A tensor-graph reduction translates low-query explored edges into vertex-cover constraints, yielding sufficient conditions through optimizable explored cores, degree moments, exploration orientations, and auxiliary degree profiles. We also derive bounds using exceptional high-degree vertices and weight-critical edges, and prove that a superconstant speedup over bidirectional Dijkstra requires all but a vanishing fraction of explored edges in each direction to concentrate around sublinear vertex sets. We also introduce a local-discovery model in which algorithms initially know only the terminal handles, cannot query undiscovered vertices or obtain the vertex count, but may make degree queries at discovered vertices. In this model, corrected bidirectional Dijkstra is constant-factor instance-optimal on directed and undirected positive-weight simple graphs, including with incoming and outgoing degree queries, for every fixed adjacency ordering. Finally, we revisit the correction to the original update rule and give a self-contained proof of the corrected multigraph guarantee.
item.dc:creator: Matic Po\v{z}ar

item.title: Learning Fourier-Sparse Signals and Multiband Signals
item.description: arXiv:2609.02977v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A classical problem in continuous sparse Fourier transforms, which dates back to Prony's work in 1795, is to learn a $k$-Fourier-sparse signal $x(t):=\sum_{j=1}^k \alpha_j e^{2 \pi \mathbf{i} f_j t}$ with arbitrary $k$ frequencies $f_1,\ldots,f_k \in \mathbb{R}$. We consider this learning problem within a fixed time window $t \in [-1,1]$ in the presence of bounded $L_2$ adversarial noise. Because the frequencies $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ can be arbitrarily close, accurately recovering individual frequencies is information-theoretically impossible even under exponentially small noise from Moitra (STOC 2015). This work therefore examines two fundamental questions: If an algorithm uses $\tilde{O}(k)$ frequencies to approximate $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ of $x$, what is the optimal covering error? And how can we efficiently learn the continuous signal $x(t)$ as a whole over the time window? Our main result is an algorithm running in time $\tilde{O}(k)$ that outputs a list $L$ of $\tilde{O}(k)$ frequencies with covering error $O(k)$ --- meaning that for most frequencies $f_j$ of $x$, $L$ guarantees $\min_{\tilde{f} \in L} |f_j-\tilde{f}| = O(k)$ --- and an reconstruction $\tilde{x}(t) \approx x(t)$ over $[-1,1]$. When constrained to outputting $\tilde{O}(k)$ frequencies, this $O(k)$ covering error is nearly optimal: Chen and Price (ICALP 2019) demonstrated two indistinguishable $k$-Fourier-sparse signals separated by distance $\tilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ in the frequency domain, which implies an amortized lower bound of $\tilde{\Omega}(k)$ per frequency. Furthermore, our sample and time complexities are nearly optimal, dramatically improving upon the previous best algorithm by Song, Sun, Weinstein, and Zhang (FOCS 2023), which required $\tilde{O}(k^4)$ samples and $\tilde{O}(k^{4\omega})$ running time.
item.dc:creator: Dongrun Cai, Xue Chen, Xiaowei Shao, Yile Wang

item.title: A Near-Linear Element-Kernel for \(d\)-Hitting Set
item.description: arXiv:2609.06512v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In \(d\)-Hitting Set, the input consists of a finite universe \(U\), a family \(\mathcal S\) of subsets of \(U\) with size at most \(d\), and an integer \(k\). The task is to decide whether at most \(k\) elements of \(U\) can intersect every set in \(\mathcal S\). Previously known kernels contain \(O(k^{d-1})\) elements and \(O(k^d)\) sets. Whether the number of elements can be reduced to \(O(k^{d-1-\varepsilon})\) for some constant \(\varepsilon>0\) is a longstanding open problem in kernelization. In this paper, we answer this question affirmatively by giving a near-linear randomized element-kernel and a subquadratic deterministic element-kernel through a re-encoding of the instance. For every fixed \(d\geq3\), we give a one-sided randomized kernel with \(O_d(k\log^3k)\) elements and a deterministic kernel with \(O_d(k^{7/4}\log^{3/2}k)\) elements. Our kernels may still contain \(k^{O(d)}\) sets and the parameter \(k\) may grow polynomially.
item.dc:creator: Zimo Sheng, Mingyu Xiao

item.title: A Sharp Barrier of Consistent Submodular Maximization: Any Improvement over $2-\sqrt{2}$ Entails Exponential Queries or Linear Recourse
item.description: arXiv:2609.09986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Consistent submodular maximization aims to maintain a high-utility subset of size at most $k$ as new elements arrive one by one, while changing only a limited number of elements per update. Previously, [DFL+25](STOC '25) established an information-theoretic bound of $2/3$ and gave the first polynomial-time randomized algorithm with a $0.51$-approximation guarantee. However, a fundamental question remained open: Is it possible to design an efficient algorithm for consistent submodular maximization that matches the classical offline $(1-1/e)$-approximation? In this paper, we answer this question in the negative by proving that the sharp approximation threshold achievable with polynomially many value queries and worst-case constant recourse is \[\beta:=2-\sqrt{2}\approx0.5858<1-1/e.\] Specifically, we develop an improved poly-time randomized algorithm, which can attain a $(\beta-\varepsilon)$-approximation in expectation at each fixed time with $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ worst-case recourse. The cornerstone of this algorithm is a novel anchored sampling scheme, which uses only value queries on subsets of the elements seen so far to construct a solution that remains competitive under unknown future arrivals. Conversely, we establish a matching lower bound by showing that any fixed improvement over $\beta$ requires either exponentially many value queries or $\Omega(k)$ changes per update. Furthermore, we characterize the impact of curvature by establishing a sharp threshold of $1-(\sqrt{2}-1)\vartheta$ for consistent submodular maximization, where $\vartheta\in[0,1]$ denotes the total curvature. Surprisingly, for weighted coverage objectives, we devise a poly-time randomized algorithm that can match the optimal $(1-1/e-\varepsilon)$-approximation with $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ worst-case recourse, thereby separating coverage maximization from general submodular maximization in the consistent settings.
item.dc:creator: Shi Fu, Qixin Zhang, Dacheng Tao

item.title: A Deadline-Driven Algorithm for Polyamorous Scheduling
item.description: arXiv:2609.10641v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In Polyamorous Scheduling Problem, we are given an edge-weighted graph and must find a periodic schedule of matchings in this graph which minimizes the maximal weighted waiting time between consecutive occurrences of the same edge. This NP-hard problem generalises Bamboo Garden Trimming and is motivated by the need to find schedules of pairwise meetings in a complex social group. We present a $4 G^*$ algorithm for Polyamorous Scheduling, improving the previously known bound of $3 + \sqrt{5} \approx 5.236$. Our algorithm is inspired by the Deadline-Driven Heuristic which is optimal for Bamboo Garden Trimming (BGT).
item.dc:creator: Arjun Maneesh Agarwal

item.title: Polynomial-time Tensor Decomposition under the Kruskal Condition and the Lovitz--Petrov Generalization
item.description: arXiv:2609.13693v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An identifiability criterion is a condition on a tensor decomposition that certifies uniqueness when the condition holds. Kruskal's classical condition is one of the best-known deterministic criteria for identifiability. However, no polynomial-time decomposition algorithm is known under the Kruskal condition; verifying the condition itself is NP-hard. Lovitz and Petrov introduced a strictly more general identifiability condition which, in contrast, is polynomial-time verifiable, but no polynomial-time decomposition algorithm was known under this condition either. In this paper we give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm, in the algebraic model over $\mathbb R$, for tensor decomposition under the Lovitz--Petrov condition, and therefore also under the stricter Kruskal condition. Moreover, combining our algorithm with polynomial-time verification of the Lovitz--Petrov condition yields an efficient end-to-end certification procedure: after computing a decomposition, one can deterministically certify in polynomial time that it is unique and therefore of minimum rank.
item.dc:creator: Shiri Sivan

item.title: Kadison--Singer in Deterministic Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2609.17266v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given rational Hermitian matrices $H_1,\dots,H_N$ of rank at most one, finds signs $s\in\{\pm1\}^N$ with $\|\sum_i s_i H_i\|\le 13\|\sum_i H_i^2\|^{1/2}$. As a corollary, for vectors $v_i$ with $\sum_i v_iv_i^*=I$ and $\|v_i\|^2\le\delta$, the signs yield a partition $[N] = S_1 \cup S_2$ such that each part satisfies $\|\sum_{i \in S_j} v_i v_i^* - \frac{I}{2}\| \leq \frac{13}{2}\sqrt\delta$ for $j = 1,2$. This gives a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the Kadison--Singer problem, in Weaver's equivalent discrepancy-theoretic $\mathsf{KS}_2$ formulation, with a universal constant.
item.dc:creator: Ekene Ezeunala, Haotian Jiang

item.title: Efficient Robust Learning at the Information-Theoretic Limit
item.description: arXiv:2609.17655v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In an important recent work, Blanc (2026) gave an algorithm for robustly learning Boolean concept classes with respect to a fixed distribution that outputs a (randomized) classifier achieving the optimal error of $\eta + \varepsilon$ where $\eta$ is the noise rate. In contrast, it is well known that deterministic hypotheses cannot achieve error less than $2\eta + \varepsilon.$ Blanc's algorithm is computationally inefficient, and the main problem left open in his work is to find a polynomial-time algorithm given access to an oracle for empirical risk minimization (ERM). In this paper, we resolve this problem and give such an algorithm. Perhaps surprisingly, our techniques make crucial use of various types of no-regret learners. Additionally, we give an efficient algorithm (no ERM oracle required) for robustly learning any function class that admits sandwiching polynomials with respect to hypercontractive distributions. As one consequence, we give the first polynomial-time algorithm for robustly learning a halfspace with respect to Gaussian marginals that achieves error $\eta + \varepsilon$ for any constant $\varepsilon$.
item.dc:creator: Adam R. Klivans, Konstantinos Stavropoulos, Sergei Tikhonov, Arsen Vasilyan

item.title: Vector Balancing in Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2609.23540v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Koml\'os problem asks for signs $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^n$ with $\|A\varepsilon\|_\infty$ bounded by an absolute constant whenever the columns of $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ have Euclidean norm at most $1$. We give the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem in the unit-cost real-RAM model. Our deterministic algorithm achieves discrepancy at most $8272$. As a consequence, we obtain a deterministic $O(\sqrt t)$-discrepancy algorithm for the Beck-Fiala problem on set systems in which each element belongs to at most $t$ sets. Our algorithm rounds a fractional coloring while keeping the row sums bounded. Its key idea is to keep the number of nearly tight row constraints small relative to the number of active coordinates. We achieve this through a spectral bound based on a weighted Gram matrix of squared row entries. We maintain the bound using a cubic spectral potential and negative-curvature updates that satisfy the required linear constraints.
item.dc:creator: Shengtao Guo, Ethan X. Fang, Junwei Lu

item.title: A Polynomial Kernel for Planar Directed Feedback Vertex Set
item.description: arXiv:2609.23669v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Directed Feedback Vertex Set problem (DFVS) asks whether a digraph can be made acyclic by deleting at most $k$ vertices. Whether DFVS admits a polynomial kernel parameterized by $k$ is a major open problem in kernelization, even for planar digraphs. We resolve the planar case by giving a deterministic kernel with $O(k^{66}\log^2 k)$ vertices and arcs. Our algorithm proceeds in three stages. First, we apply structural reduction rules to the input digraph, bounding the number of directed faces and some special vertices. Second, we pass to the planar dual, where vertex deletion corresponds to adding groups of reverse arcs to make each weakly connected component strongly connected. The structural bounds in the first stage yield a small retained vertex set in the dual. We then compress the dual instance by identifying vertices with the same distance records from this retained vertex set. The main technical contribution is a directed-cut argument showing that this identification preserves feasibility. Finally, we transform the polynomial-size dual instance back into an instance of Planar Directed Feedback Vertex Set via a $3$-CNF encoding and a planar graph construction.
item.dc:creator: Zimo Sheng, Mingyu Xiao

item.title: A Constructive FPT Algorithm for Integer Cone Optimization with Convex Costs
item.description: arXiv:2609.31328v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic fixed-parameter algorithm for integer cone optimization with convex costs. Given $\tau$ rational polytopes in $\R^{d+k}$, we combine generators whose first $d$ coordinates are integral and whose remaining $k$ coordinates may be fractional. Each generator has a convex cost depending only on its integer coordinates. We minimize the total cost of nonnegative integer combinations subject to arbitrary rational linear constraints on the full typewise aggregates and generator counts. Our algorithm runs in time \[ 2^{\tau\log(\tau+1)\,2^{O(d)}}\cdot |I|^{O(1)}, \] where $|I|$ is the total binary input length. It constructs an optimal representation using at most $2^{2d+1}$ distinct generators per type. The number $k$ of continuous coordinates contributes only to the polynomial input factor. For a single generator type, the running time becomes $2^{2^{O(d)}}\cdot |I|^{O(1)}$. Applications include constructive FPT algorithms for Cone and Polytope Intersection, high-multiplicity bin packing, vector bin packing, and makespan minimization on uniform and unrelated machines. The double-exponential dependence on $d$ is tight for Point-in-Cone and both bin-packing problems assuming $\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{SUBEXP}$. The mixed-integer formulation also yields additive EPTASs for makespan minimization, machine covering, and envy minimization on identical machines, and additive schemes fixed-parameter tractable in $1/\varepsilon+\tau$ on uniform machines.
item.dc:creator: Klaus Jansen, Felix Ohnesorge, Bj\"orn Schumacher

item.title: Hermite Brings a Laptop: Analyzing Frieze-Jerrum Rounding Yields Improved Approximations for Clustering Problems
item.description: arXiv:2609.35453v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Frieze-Jerrum rounding is a standard tool for rounding SDP relaxations of graph partitioning and clustering problems, assigning nodes to at most $k$ clusters using $k$ independent Gaussian vectors. Its analysis hinges on the collision probability $P_k(\rho)$ that two nodes whose SDP vectors have inner product $\rho$ are assigned to the same cluster. No tractable closed form for $P_k$ is known for $k\geq 4$, making it difficult to certify approximation guarantees and hindering the systematic search for better algorithms. We develop a Hermite-coefficient certification framework to derive accurate and tractable bounds on $P_k$. Using the Hermite expansion of Gaussian noise stability, we express $P_k$ as a power series with nonnegative coefficients, reduce these coefficients to one-dimensional Gaussian integrals, and certify finitely many of them, yielding rigorous bounds on $P_k$ over the entire correlation range. Our framework yields strengthened polynomial-time approximations for several clustering problems. For MaxAgree Correlation Clustering, we derive a $0.7818$-approximation, the first improvement in two decades over the $0.7666$ ratio of Swamy (2004). We also improve the best known ratios for the variant with at most $K$ clusters, MaxAgree$[K]$ (e.g., from $0.77$ to $0.8151$ for $K=3$). For Max $K$-Cut we resolve, via a structural property of the Hermite expansion, a conjecture of de Klerk et al. (2004) characterizing the Frieze--Jerrum approximation ratio for every $K\ge3$; we show that this ratio is tight, and determine it to within $10^{-6}$ accuracy for $K\le16$. Finally, we reduce the additive approximation error for modularity maximization from $0.42084$ (Kawase et al., 2021) to $0.3790$. On the hardness side, we show that approximating Maxagree within $0.802+\epsilon$ is Unique Games-hard via a construction in Gaussian space analyzed by Borell's inequality.
item.dc:creator: David Garc\'ia-Soriano, Atsushi Miyauchi

item.title: An FPRAS for Counting Common Bases of Two Matroids
item.description: arXiv:2610.06724v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We design the first fully polynomial-time randomized approximation scheme ($\mathsf{FPRAS}$) for approximately counting and uniformly sampling common bases of two matroids given by their independence oracles. Moreover, our algorithms generalize far beyond this to Hadamard products of two probability measures on the Boolean cube satisfying a simple nonnegative curvature condition. These algorithmic primitives have myriad applications in statistical physics, polyhedral combinatorics, the theory of quantum many-body systems, and beyond. The central difficulty is that the hard constraints imposed by the two input matroids (or the two input measures, more generally) obstruct traditional approaches based on local Markov chains. Relaxing these constraints can restore rapid mixing, but configurations that satisfy the original hard constraints may become exponentially rare if this is done na\"ively. Our main contribution is a novel approach for approximate counting that marries Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) with convex programming to overcome these obstacles: - We relax the intersection by imposing an overlap penalty on the product measure formed by the two input measures. We prove, via an integrated Bochner-type method, that this "soft intersection" satisfies a Poincar\'e Inequality uniformly over all external fields. - We use samples from the relaxed distribution to solve a dual maximum entropy convex program inspired by the Gurvits capacity. This program reweights the soft intersection measure using external fields to boost the aggregate probability of configurations satisfying the hard intersection constraint, without changing their relative weights. We bound the success probability directly using the uniform Poincar\'e Inequality and smallness of the gradient norm. AI Disclosure: GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra and GPT-6 Astra Ultra were heavily used to develop the ideas in this paper.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Chen, Kuikui Liu

item.title: Nearly optimal Personalized PageRank computation
item.description: arXiv:2610.06959v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the fundamental problem of computing Personalized PageRank (PPR) on an undirected and unweighted graph $G$. We focus on the $\eps$-error guarantee introduced by Andersen, Chung, and Lang [ACL; FOCS 2006 $\&$ Internet Math 2007]. Their classic local push method computes an approximate PPR vector satisfying the ACL $\eps$-error guarantee in $O((\alpha\eps)^{-1})$ time, where $\alpha$ is the teleportation parameter. This problem has a lower bound $\Omega(\eps^{-1})$. Working with idealized SDDM solves, we eliminate the dependence on $\alpha$ and present an algorithm that achieves the same error guarantee in $O(\eps^{-1-o(1)})$ time. Consequently, we obtain a nearly optimal algorithm for PPR computation under the ACL error guarantee, and a nearly linear algorithm for local graph clustering with complexity independent of $\phi$.
item.dc:creator: Rong-Hua Li, Quanqing Xu, Yichun Yang, Junjie Zhou

item.title: Unconditional Boolean Dynamic Lower Bounds from Disjointness
item.description: arXiv:2610.10904v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We prove an unconditional $\Omega((\log n/\log\log n)^2)$ lower bound on the maximum of the worst-case update time and expected query time for the insert-only version of Patrascu's multiphase Disjointness problem [STOC 2010]. The bound holds in the zero-error cell-probe model with logarithmic word size. Patrascu's reductions transfer it to directed reachability under edge insertions, already on directed acyclic graphs of depth $2$. This improves the $\widetilde{\Omega}(\log^{3/2} n)$ bound of Larsen and Yu [SICOMP 2025] to the quadratic-logarithmic scale previously attained for dynamic range counting and multiphase Inner Product. The bound also transfers to a broad collection of dynamic graph, algebraic, geometric, and string problems. We also obtain a separation between amortized and worst-case time for streaming regular-expression membership. For a simple family of expressions of maximum length $M$ over a polynomial-size alphabet, a deterministic algorithm uses $O(1)$ amortized time per symbol on every input stream, whereas every zero-error cell-probe algorithm with word size $w=\Theta(\log M)$ requires $\Omega((\log M/\log\log M)^2)$ time on some symbol. The proof adapts Ko's 2.5-round multiphase communication framework [FOCS 2026] from Inner Product to Disjointness. Our main technical observation is that the protocol's verification step allows a one-sided corruption bound to replace the discrepancy property used for Inner Product.
item.dc:creator: Young Kun Ko

item.title: QPTAS for Max Weight Independent Set in Graphs with Strongly Edge-Sublinear Separators
item.description: arXiv:2610.16025v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A hereditary graph class has strongly edge-sublinear separators if, for some constant $0 \leqslant b < 1$, every graph in the class with $m$ edges admits a balanced separator of size $\mathcal O(m^b)$. We show that Max Weight Independent Set (MWIS) admits a deterministic quasipolynomial-time approximation scheme (QPTAS) on every such class. In particular, this applies to graphs excluding any fixed graph as an induced minor, by a separator theorem of Korhonen and Lokshtanov [SODA 2024]. Our theorem generalizes the QPTASes for axis-parallel rectangles [Adamaszek and Wiese, FOCS 2013] and polygons [Adamaszek, Har-Peled, and Wiese, JACM 2019], or equivalently for packing connected subgraphs of a planar graph [Pilipczuk, van Leeuwen, and Wiese, Algorithmica 2020]. It also generalizes the QPTAS for MWIS on hereditary classes with strongly sublinear separators measured in vertices [Dvo\v{r}\'ak, EJC 2018; Dvo\v{r}\'ak and Lahiri, ESA 2021], as well as the QPTASes for graphs excluding specific induced minors [Chudnovsky et al., arXiv 2025; Bonnet et al., SWAT 2026; Czy\.zewska et al., arXiv 2026].
item.dc:creator: \'Edouard Bonnet, Yeonsu Chang

item.title: Exact minimum Birkhoff decompositions of doubly stochastic matrices with finite precision
item.description: arXiv:2610.25837v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The minimum Birkhoff decomposition problem asks for a representation of a doubly stochastic matrix as a convex combination of as few permutation matrices as possible. This NP-hard problem arises in the scheduling of switches in data centers and satellite systems, in random assignments in economics and in the statistics of rankings. We consider doubly stochastic matrices whose entries are given with a fixed number of decimal digits and look for exact decompositions whose weights have the same precision. We propose a parallel method with three parts. For matrices built from few permutation matrices, the first part reads the weights from the frequencies of the entries and places them on the matrix positions by a rule that, given the correct weights, never fixes a position wrongly. The second part computes lower bounds from pairs of rows or columns, which remain valid for real weights, and from certificates of a satisfiability solver. For matrices built from many permutation matrices, the third part runs a beam search over steps that each make at least one entry zero. On 375 test instances with up to 100 rows, the method proves optimality for 208 instances, and 197 of these proofs also hold for real weights. Of the 190 instances built from few permutation matrices, 187 are solved to proven optimality, 180 of them within one second. Compared with the best exact decompositions known before, the new decompositions are shorter for 278 instances and never longer.
item.dc:creator: Andr\'as Cz\'egel

item.title: Approximation Algorithms for Directed Telephone Multicast
item.description: arXiv:2610.27422v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Telephone multicast is a classical problem in information dissemination. In the directed setting, a message starts at a source in an $n$-vertex digraph, and each informed vertex may call one out-neighbour per round. The goal is to inform a given set of $k$ terminals in the fewest rounds. Despite previous work on telephone multicast, a substantial approximation gap remained in the directed setting: approximating the problem within a factor of $o(\log k)$ is NP-hard, while the best existing polynomial-time approximation guarantee depending only on $k$ was $\widetilde O(\sqrt{k})$. For every integer $\ell\ge2$, we give a deterministic combinatorial algorithm that runs in $n^{O(\ell)}$ time and returns a schedule of length $O(\ell^3\log k)(OPT+k^{1/\ell})$, where $OPT$ is the optimum number of rounds. This yields an $O(k^\epsilon)$ approximation in time $n^{O(1/\epsilon)}$ for every fixed $\epsilon>0$, and an $O(\log^4 k)$ approximation in quasi-polynomial time. The same algorithm gives an $O(\log k)$ approximation whenever $OPT\ge k^\epsilon$ for a fixed $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, which is optimal up to a constant factor unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$. On planar digraphs, we obtain a deterministic polynomial-time $O(\log^2 k)$ approximation. More generally, we give an $O(p\log^2 k)$ approximation for minor-closed graph classes with the following separator property. Given any rooted spanning tree, a balanced separator can be computed in polynomial time as the union of all vertices on at most $p$ tree paths from the root to chosen vertices. Classes of bounded treewidth satisfy this property. We also strengthen the known logarithmic approximation hardness for directed telephone multicast, extending it from instances with a polynomially large optimum to instances with $OPT=O(\log k)$.
item.dc:creator: Shahin Kamali, Seyed-Mohammad Seyed-Javadi

item.title: A Linear Lower Bound for Convex Body Chasing in Every Norm
item.description: arXiv:2610.32670v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We establish an $\Omega(d)$ lower bound on the competitive ratio of convex body chasing in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with movement costs measured in any norm. Previously, the best known lower bound valid across all norms was $\Omega(d^{1/6})$, established by Papazov (2023); stronger lower bounds were known for $\ell_p$ norms, where Bubeck, Klartag, Lee, Li, and Sellke (2019) had established a lower bound of $\Omega(\max\{\sqrt{d}, d^{1-1/p}\})$. In particular, a linear lower bound was known only for the $\ell_\infty$ norm, realized by the standard construction of chasing faces of a hypercube. Our lower bound strictly improves on the prior universal and $\ell_p$ lower bounds for $p < \infty$ and shows that the functional Steiner point algorithm of Sellke (2023) - which has competitive ratio $O(d)$ - is asymptotically optimal for every norm. Our approach is based on the recursive construction of Bubeck, Coester, and Rabani (2023) for metrical service systems, which gives a lower bound of $\Omega(r^2)$ for requests of size $O(r)$. We show that requests in their construction, each comprising a set of discrete points in a graph metric, can be mapped to the vertices of convex requests in a $(2r+1)$-dimensional $\ell_p$ vector space while approximately preserving movement costs up to a factor of $O(r)$; the general result then follows via Milman's (1985) quotient-of-a-subspace theorem.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Christianson

item.title: Deterministic Incremental Triconnectivity in $O(\log^2 n)$ Worst-Case Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.32721v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the problem of maintaining the triconnectivity in a graph $G$ in the incremental dynamic setting. We consider updates in the form of edge insertions and edge subdivisions, and triconnectivity queries, i.e. queries that take as input variables the vertices $a$ and $b$ and are of the form ''are there at least three vertex disjoint paths between $a$ and $b$?''. All algorithms presented in this paper are deterministic. When starting from a biconnected graph, all updates take worst-case $O(\log n)$ time, and all queries are answered in $O(\log n)$ time. By combining this result for biconnected graphs with a result of Holm and Rotenberg [SODA'20] we get a deterministic algorithm for general graphs with a worst-case update and query time of $O(\log^2 n)$. Both algorithms represent an improvement of the state-of-the-art by a factor of $O(\log n)$.
item.dc:creator: Niels Inselmann Christiansen, Eva Rotenberg

item.title: Tight Coreset Bounds for $(k,z)$-Clustering in Euclidean and Doubling Metrics
item.description: arXiv:2610.34373v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We determine the optimal worst-case size of strong coresets for $(k,z)$-clustering in Euclidean spaces and doubling metrics, up to polylogarithmic factors. In Euclidean space, previous lower bounds matched the best upper bounds only for $\varepsilon\gtrsim k^{-1/(z+2)}$. We close the gap for arbitrarily small $\varepsilon$, establishing the optimal size $\widetilde\Theta(\min\{k^{(2z+2)/(z+2)}\varepsilon^{-2},\,k\varepsilon^{-z-2}\})$ for every fixed $z\ge1$, all $k\ge1$, and $0<\varepsilon<1$. Our lower bound replaces each offset in a previous hard instance by a group of distinct offsets. A fixed family of $k$-center queries and four-wise independent signs force a large relative cost error for every sufficiently small subset with arbitrary nonnegative weights. For doubling metrics of dimension $D$, we resolve the previously unmatched bounds for $z>2$. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde O(k^{2-2/z}D\varepsilon^{-2})$ and a lower bound that, together with known upper bounds, establishes the optimal size $\widetilde\Theta(kD\min\{k^{1-2/z}\varepsilon^{-2},\,\varepsilon^{-z}\})$ for fixed $z>2$, $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_z$, and $D\ge C_z\log(2/\varepsilon)$, where $C_z>0$ and $\varepsilon_z\in(0,1)$ depend only on $z$. The lower bound exploits the ability to encode $\Theta(D)$ independent signs per center without diluting relative cost discrepancy. For the upper bound, we use independent, unbiased two-point summaries that exactly preserve cluster mass and anchor cost, combined with iterative size reduction.
item.dc:creator: Junqiu Hu, Lingxiao Huang, Jian Li, Baoduo Xu

item.title: Zero-freeness for Random Regular Graphs up to the Replica Symmetry Breaking Threshold
item.description: arXiv:2610.40510v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study antiferromagnetic spin systems on random regular graphs through the lens of the phase transitions characterized by the complex zeros of the partition function. Our motivating examples include the hardcore model and the antiferromagnetic Potts model (including proper $q$-colorings at $\beta=0$). For both models on random $d$-regular graphs, we establish, with high probability over the graph, zero-free regions throughout the interior of the replica-symmetric regime. Asymptotically, this regime extends up to tree occupation density $$\alpha < \alpha_{\mathrm{RSB}}(d) = (2\log d - 2\log\log d + 2 - 2\log 2 + o_d(1))/d$$ for the hardcore model and up to degree $$d < d_{\mathrm{RSB}}(q) = (2q-1)\log q - 2\log 2 + o_q(1)$$ for proper $q$-colorings. Leveraging the standard algorithmic implications of zero-freeness, we obtain deterministic polynomial-time algorithms that multiplicatively approximate the corresponding partition functions at fixed rational parameters throughout this regime, with high probability over the graph. Our algorithmic guarantees significantly improve upon prior work and extend beyond the parameter ranges reached by previously known search algorithms. As a key intermediate step, we establish the pointwise equivalence, away from the threshold, of three notions of replica symmetry: geometric (averaged pairwise correlation decay), thermodynamic (convergence to the Bethe free-energy prediction), and variational (nonpositivity of the Bethe functional). To establish zero-freeness, we develop reinforced small subgraph conditioning, lifting classical small subgraph conditioning to random holomorphic functions to control short-cycle fluctuations. We also use variational replica symmetry to obtain exponential planted overlap concentration. This enables a typical-graph truncation that controls complex second moments up to the replica symmetry breaking threshold.
item.dc:creator: Zejia Chen, Chunyang Wang, Xinyuan Zhang

item.title: Testing MAX-CUT in the Adjacency Matrix Model: Tight Non-Adaptive Bounds and a Cubic Adaptive Lower Bound
item.description: arXiv:2611.00682v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the query complexity of approximating the MAX-CUT value to additive error $\varepsilon n^2$ in the adjacency matrix model. This was one of the first problems studied in graph property testing [GGR'98]. Previously, the best known upper bound for both adaptive and non-adaptive algorithms was $O(1/\varepsilon^6)$ [RV'07; MS'08; GMRS'22]. The only known lower bound was a trivial $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^2)$ bound. We close this gap from both sides for non-adaptive algorithms, proving that its query complexity is exactly $\Theta(1/\varepsilon^4)$. We also prove an adaptive $\Omega(1/\varepsilon^3)$ lower bound. Our upper bound is achieved by a canonical tester that samples $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ vertices in expectation and outputs the rescaled MAX-CUT value of the induced subgraph. We prove its correctness by applying spectral truncation to the adjacency matrix, using a geometric argument to control the sampling error of the retained low-rank part and a cut-norm restriction estimate [RV'07] for the remainder. As an application, an analogous proof also yields a tight $O(1/\varepsilon^4)$ non-adaptive query upper bound for MAX-2CSP. For our lower bounds, we show indistinguishability between a uniform random graph and a random graph with a planted hidden partition. For the non-adaptive lower bound, we observe that one plus the $\chi^2$-divergence between the query transcript distributions is exactly a normalized Ising partition function, which can be bounded using Boolean hypercontractivity. For the adaptive lower bound, we relate each query's distinguishing power to the prediction, based on previous answers, of whether its endpoints lie in the same part of the hidden partition. We bound the combined advantage of these predictions using the completed transcript, which lets us analyze the adaptively chosen pairs of vertices together despite their dependence on earlier answers.
item.dc:creator: Songhua He

item.title: Exact Tie-Breaking and Tight Degree Bounds for Minimum-Degree Greedy on Interval Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.01796v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study tie-breaking in the minimum-degree greedy algorithm (MDG) for maximum independent set on interval graphs. Given an interval representation of an $n$-vertex graph, we compute the largest and smallest output sizes and construct executions attaining them in $O(n^3)$ time and $O(n^2)$ space. For maximum degree at most four, favorable tie-breaking gives a tight guarantee of $3/4$. For every maximum-degree bound of at least five, the guarantee drops to $2/3$. Both bounds are tight even on connected unit interval graphs whose output size is independent of tie-breaking. Together with the known optimality of favorable tie-breaking for maximum degree at most three, these results give a complete classification by degree bound.
item.dc:creator: Ruize Zhao

item.title: Finding and Certifying Weighted Minimum Cuts with Cut Queries
item.description: arXiv:2611.03107v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the deterministic and nondeterministic cut query complexity of minimum cut in undirected graphs with arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. For the nondeterministic case, we show that every $n$-vertex graph has an $O(n\log^2(2n))$-query certificate of its exact global minimum-cut value, such that any other nonnegatively weighted graph on the same vertex set that agrees on these queries has the same minimum cut value. A key ingredient is a way to certify a maximum $s$--$t$ flow value with only $O(n)$ cut queries. For the deterministic case we give an algorithm that finds an exact global minimum cut using $O(n^{3/2}\log^3(2n)(\log\log(2n))^2)$ cut queries. Previously no $O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ deterministic bound was known for arbitrary nonnegatively weighted graphs. The algorithm follows Karger's two-respecting tree approach. The key new ingredient is a deterministic construction of a weak skeleton of the input graph $G$: an explicit weighted graph $H$ in which every minimum cut of $G$ is a $5/4$-approximate minimum cut.
item.dc:creator: Troy Lee

item.title: Towards Optimal Multi-draft Speculative Decoding
item.description: arXiv:2502.18779v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become an indispensable part of natural language processing tasks. However, autoregressive sampling has become an efficiency bottleneck. Multi-Draft Speculative Decoding (MDSD) is a recent approach where, when generating each token, a small draft model generates multiple drafts, and the target LLM verifies them in parallel, ensuring that the final output conforms to the target model distribution. The two main design choices in MDSD are the draft sampling method and the verification algorithm. For a fixed draft sampling method, the optimal acceptance rate is a solution to an optimal transport problem, but the complexity of this problem makes it difficult to solve for the optimal acceptance rate and measure the gap between existing verification algorithms and the theoretical upper bound. This paper discusses the dual of the optimal transport problem, providing a way to efficiently compute the optimal acceptance rate. For the first time, we measure the theoretical upper bound of MDSD efficiency for vocabulary sizes in the thousands and quantify the gap between existing verification algorithms and this bound. We also compare different draft sampling methods based on their optimal acceptance rates. Our results show that the draft sampling method strongly influences the optimal acceptance rate, with sampling without replacement outperforming sampling with replacement.
