Additionally, existing verification algorithms do not reach the theoretical upper bound for both without replacement and with replacement sampling. Our findings suggest that carefully designed draft sampling methods can potentially improve the optimal acceptance rate and enable the development of verification algorithms that closely match the theoretical upper bound.
item.dc:creator: Zhengmian Hu, Tong Zheng, Vignesh Viswanathan, Ziyi Chen, Ryan A. Rossi, Yihan Wu, Dinesh Manocha, Heng Huang

item.title: On the average-case complexity landscape for Tensor-Isomorphism-complete problems over finite fields
item.description: arXiv:2604.00591v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In Grochow and Qiao (\emph{SIAM J. Comput.}, 2023), the complexity class Tensor Isomorphism (TI) was introduced and isomorphism problems for groups, algebras, and polynomials were shown to be TI-complete. In this paper, we study average-case algorithms for several TI-complete problems over finite fields, including algebra isomorphism, matrix code conjugacy, and $4$-tensor isomorphism. Our main results reveal a rich landscape of average-case complexities of Tensor Isomorphism problems, despite their equivalence in the worst-case setting. Over the finite field of order $q$, we devise (1) average-case \emph{polynomial-time} algorithms for algebra isomorphism and matrix code conjugacy that succeed for $1/\Theta(q)$ fraction of inputs; (2) an average-case \emph{polynomial-time} algorithm for the $4$-tensor isomorphism that succeeds for $1/q^{\Theta(1)}$ fraction of inputs; and (3) an average-case \emph{polynomial-time} algorithm for the orthogonal $3$-tensor isomorphism that succeed for $1-1/\poly(n)$ fraction of $n\times n\times n$ tensors. Our main technical contribution is to introduce the spectral properties of random matrices into algorithms for TI-complete problems. This leads to not only new algorithms but also new questions in random matrix theory over finite fields. To settle these questions, we need to extend both the generating function approach as in Neumann and Praeger (\emph{J. London Math. Soc.}, 1998) and the character sum method of Gorodetsky and Rodgers (\emph{Trans. Amer. Math. Soc.}, 2021).
item.dc:creator: Tiange Li, Yinan Li, Youming Qiao, Dacheng Tao, Yingjie Wang

item.title: Low-Degree Learning from Localization Schemes
item.description: arXiv:2604.06109v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The low-degree algorithm is a cornerstone in computational learning theory. For product or Gaussian distributions, it shows that efficiently learnability follows from Fourier concentration. However, a longstanding obstacle towards building such a theory over nonproduct distributions is that we can no longer rely on having closed-form expressions for a good basis of orthogonal functions. This hints that the analysis of the low-degree algorithm might be brittle to the underlying distributional assumptions. We refute this intuition by showing that the low-degree algorithm provably succeeds for a large class of graphical models under mild high-temperature conditions. As an application, for nearly every Ising model that is known to rapidly mix, we obtain learning algorithms for every function class for which the Fourier approach succeeds for product distributions (e.g. low-depth circuits, halfspaces, intersections, monotone, among others) with no significant loss. Our framework is based on a strikingly clean connection with the coordinate-by-coordinate localization scheme of Chen and Eldan introduced for establishing rapid mixing in high-temperature models, as well as other analytical transference principles to product distributions.
item.dc:creator: Gautam Chandrasekaran, Jason Gaitonde, Ankur Moitra, Arsen Vasilyan

item.title: Constant-factor approximation of MinCostCSP with a conservative majority polymorphism
item.description: arXiv:2607.10667v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For a relational structure A, the Minimum Cost Constraint Satisfaction Problem is the following problem denoted by MinCostCSP(A): Given an instance of CSP(A) with rational costs on variable-value pairs, find a solution to the instance minimizing the sum of the chosen costs. For the exact minimization, a classification of MinCostCSP(A) in terms of A was established by Takhanov [STACS'10]. We focus on constant-factor approximations of MinCostCSP(A). DeHaan, Huang, and Lee recently showed that if A fails to admit a conservative near-unanimity polymorphism then MinCostCSP(A) is not constant-factor approximable [APPROX'25]. We provide a significant step towards a full classification, by proving a dichotomy for structures A admitting a conservative majority (also known as 3-near-unanimity) polymorphism. Our dichotomy criterion is not in terms of an algebraic condition on A but we show that this is unavoidable. We include a simple argument proving that no such condition exists.
item.dc:creator: Marcin Kozik, Stanislav \v{Z}ivn\'y

item.title: Online Beck--Fiala Down to Logarithmic Sparsity
item.description: arXiv:2607.14238v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The celebrated (offline) Beck--Fiala conjecture asserts that every matrix $A\in\{0,1\}^{n\times T}$ with at most $d$ nonzero entries in each column has discrepancy $O(\sqrt d)$. In this note, we consider the {\it online} version of the conjecture. For every fixed $\eta>0$, we give a randomized online algorithm that achieves $O_\eta(\sqrt d)$ prefix discrepancy for every fixed sequence of $d$-sparse vectors $a_t\in[-1,1]^n$, except with probability at most \[ C_\eta T\exp\left[-\frac{c_\eta d}{\log^{2+\eta}(ed)}\right]. \] In particular, this gives an optimal $O(\sqrt d)$ discrepancy upper bound for $d\geq C_\eta(\log T)(\log\log T)^{2+\eta}$. This range of sparsity is optimal up to $\log\log T$ factors. The result also resolves in strong form the {\it online Spencer problem}, corresponding to the case $d = n$. The algorithm is based on a compactly supported Metropolis walk, constructed by combining ideas from several recent works on online vector balancing. The proof was generated in conversation with ChatGPT 5.6 Pro; the authors provided high-level guidance in several rounds of prompting, followed by manual checking and rewriting of the proof.
item.dc:creator: Dylan J. Altschuler, Konstantin Tikhomirov

item.title: Learning Arbitrary Lindbladians from Time Evolution
item.description: arXiv:2607.28610v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the problem of learning arbitrary $n$-qubit Lindbladians, the generators of Markovian open-system dynamics, from their time evolution. We give the first known efficient algorithm that learns arbitrary Lindbladians without any structural assumptions. For an $n$-qubit Lindbladian of dynamical strength at most $\Lambda$, the algorithm estimates every coefficient to error $\varepsilon$ using $\widetilde O(\Lambda^2/\varepsilon^2)$ experiments and $\widetilde O(\Lambda/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, with classical running time polynomial in $n$ and $\Lambda/\varepsilon$. Both experimental costs match known lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. The algorithm identifies candidate labels through product Pauli experiments and estimates their coefficients using random stabilizer preparations and Clifford measurements. It requires no ancillas or control during the unknown evolution. For constant $k$, our algorithm learns generic $k$-local Lindbladians of local dynamical strength at most $\Lambda_{\mathrm{loc}}$ using $\widetilde O(n^2\Lambda_{\mathrm{loc}}^2/\varepsilon^2)$ experiments and $\widetilde O(n\Lambda_{\mathrm{loc}}/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, improving the upper bounds of prior works in terms of the dependence on $n$. We further improve the lower bounds of Arad, Chen, Guo, Rebentrost, and Yu (SODA 2027) using a family of $3$-local Lindbladians. They already hold when the support is known, and only one Hamiltonian coefficient is requested, even for adaptive protocols with arbitrary ancillas and quantum memory. These lower bounds establish that our algorithm is optimal up to polylogarithmic factors in both experiment count and total evolution time for every fixed $k \geq 3$.
item.dc:creator: Zhili Chen, Zhan Yu

item.title: Rigorous Low-Degree Implications for Planted Subgraph Detection: Noise and Treewidth
item.description: arXiv:2608.06279v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The low-degree method predicts computational thresholds by asking whether low-degree polynomials can distinguish a planted distribution from a null one. Recent counterexamples by Buhai, Hsieh, Jain, and Kothari (FOCS 2025) and Mao (2026) show that low-degree indistinguishability does not, in general, rule out efficient algorithms, even on noisy inputs. Hsieh, Kane, Kothari, Li, Mohanty, and Tiegel (STOC 2026) asked what it does imply, and showed that for permutation-invariant distributions on $\{0,1\}^n$, low-degree indistinguishability from the uniform distribution implies statistical indistinguishability after noise. In this work, we study the same question for planted subgraphs in sparse random graphs. Let $Q_n=G(n,c/n)$, and let $P_n$ be obtained by planting a uniformly random copy of a deterministic graph $\Gamma_n$ into an independent sample from $Q_n$. In the supercritical regime $c>1$, we show that if $P_n$ is degree-$D_n$ indistinguishable from $Q_n$ and the treewidth of $\Gamma_n$ is $o(D_n/\log n)$, then a noisy version of $P_n$ is asymptotically indistinguishable from $Q_n$. In the critical and subcritical regimes $0<c\le 1$, we obtain the same conclusion without any treewidth assumption, provided $D_n=\omega(\log n)$. Our proof has two main ingredients. First, we identify the subgraph-count and automorphism factors in the Fourier expansion with counts of isomorphism triples. Second, we cut a tree decomposition of $\Gamma_n$ into subtrees, which splits each large Fourier support into low-degree pieces that meet at only a few interface vertices, and we use noise to absorb the cost of reassembling them. At and below criticality, we use the low-degree assumption to rule out short cycles and noise to destroy the remaining long ones.
item.dc:creator: Xuan Chen, Shuangping Li

item.title: Max Independent Set Remains NP-hard when Excluding a Planar Induced Minor (and More)
item.description: arXiv:2609.11285v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We show that Max Independent Set (MIS) remains NP-hard in graphs excluding the $5 \times 5$ grid as an induced minor. This negatively answers a question of Dallard--Milani\v{c}--\v{S}torgel that has attracted sustained attention, and refutes a conjecture by Gartland and Lokshtanov. Unless $N$-variable 3-SAT can be solved in time $2^{\mathcal O(N^{1-\varepsilon})}$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$, MIS requires $2^{\Omega(n^{1/2-o(1)})}$ time on $n$-vertex graphs in this class. This complements a $2^{\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})}$-time algorithm on any $H$-induced-minor-free class by Korhonen and Lokshtanov. Exploiting a connection between low twin-width or reduced parameters on one hand and planar-induced-minor-freeness on the other, we further show that 3-Coloring, Feedback Vertex Set and Dominating Set are NP-complete on weakly sparse graphs of reduced component max-leaf (hence twin-width) at most 3, even when a witnessing contraction sequence is given. Classes of bounded reduced component max-leaf (by any constant) and of twin-width at most 3 are known to exclude a fixed planar graph as an induced minor. The 3-Coloring and Feedback Vertex Set results refute more cases of the Gartland--Lokshtanov conjecture, even when the inputs are weakly sparse. The complexity of MIS in weakly sparse graphs excluding a planar induced minor remains open.
item.dc:creator: \'Edouard Bonnet, Yeonsu Chang

item.title: Free-Probabilistic State Evolution and Random Matrix Discrepancy
item.description: arXiv:2609.11836v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Let $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ be independent $d \times d$ real symmetric Gaussian random matrices, and consider the linear operator $A(x) = n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i$, $x\in \mathbb R^n$. We construct an iterative algorithm in the Approximate Message Passing family which iterates over $A$ and its adjoint $A^*$, and establish a state evolution result which characterizes its behavior in the limit $d\to \infty, 2n/d^2 \to \alpha$ in terms of a correlated Gaussian-semicircular process in a free probability space, in the sense of strong convergence of operators. We then apply this iteration to the random matrix discrepancy problem which asks for a binary vector $x \in \{-1,+1\}^n$ such that $A(x)$ has a small operator norm. Our algorithm achieves an operator norm $2\sigma(\alpha)$, for a standard deviation $\sigma(\alpha)<1$ for all $\alpha>0$, and $\sigma(\alpha) = O(1/\sqrt{\alpha \log \alpha})$ for large $\alpha$. This resolves the algorithmic question of Kunisky-Zhang (2023) and Maillard (2025).
item.dc:creator: August Y. Chen, Ahmed El Alaoui

item.title: A Cheeger Inequality for Hypergraphs and Its Applications
item.description: arXiv:2609.16286v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hypergraphs provide a natural framework for modeling higher-order relationships, but the development of spectral techniques with provable guarantees for general non-uniform hypergraphs remains challenging. Building on Banerjee's normalized adjacency matrix and Spiro's averaging-based diffusion framework, we develop a spectral framework for non-uniform hypergraphs and establish Cheeger's inequality for their conductance. A fundamental result in the spectral theory of hypergraphs asserts that, for every non-covering hypergraph, the second-smallest eigenvalue of its normalized Laplacian is at most one. This spectral characterization yields an improved Cheeger's inequality for non-covering hypergraphs, and we show that the resulting inequality is tight on both sides using cycle and cube hypergraphs. Our framework further yields higher-order Cheeger inequalities and provides theoretical guarantees for Fiedler's spectral partitioning algorithm, all in the setting of hypergraphs. Finally and most notably, we construct a new family of optimal hypergraph expanders that is tight for the Alon-Boppana bound.
item.dc:creator: Raj Kamal, Amitabha Bagchi

item.title: A Fixed-Parameter Algorithm for 4-Block Integer Programming
item.description: arXiv:2609.23711v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We give a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm with running time $f(k,\bar\Delta)\cdot {|I|}^{O(1)}$ for integer linear programs with 4-block structure, parameterized by the maximum block dimension $k$ and the largest absolute entry $\bar\Delta$ in the local-column blocks. This result resolves a long-standing open question in parameterized complexity, and answers a conjecture by Eisenbrand and Rothvoss (2026) in the positive. This result has several implications for other block-structured integer programming models, including mixed fracture number and special cases of 4-block programs with large entries outside of the diagonal. Important tools for this algorithm are structural properties of generalized $n$-fold integer programs shown by Ligthart~(2026) and an algorithm by Veselov, Gribanov, Zolotykh and Chirkov~(2020) for optimizing discrete convic functions. Independently and shortly after the first version of our paper appeared, Kouteck\'y, Lassota, and Ligthart (2026) obtained an FPT algorithm for 4-block integer programming.
item.dc:creator: Klaus Jansen, Felix Ohnesorge, Corinna Wambsganz

item.title: Single-or-Sample: Online Fair Allocation for Combinatorial Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.32286v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the fair allocation of $m$ indivisible goods among $n$ heterogeneous agents arriving online, under maximin share (MMS) fairness. The key challenge lies in making allocation decisions in an adversarial setting without knowing future agents' valuations. No guarantees were known prior to our work in adversarial settings. Our main positive result is an online allocation algorithm for submodular agents that with probability at least $0.4$ guarantees a $1/24$-approximation to MMS to all agents simultaneously. Our algorithm intersperses a greedy-style adaptive sampling-without-replacement protocol with single-good reduction rounds. For XOS valuations, we adapt this single-or-sample approach to guarantee a $c$-MMS for all agents simultaneously with probability $1-O(c)$ for any parameter $c\in O(1/\log n)$. A key technical contribution of our work is in establishing Chernoff-style tail bounds on item allocation events for this adaptive sampling process despite strong positive correlations among the items, a result that may be of independent interest. The approximation versus success probability tradeoffs achieved by our algorithms are asymptotically tight. We show that even for binary additive valuations, no randomized algorithm can ensure $c$-MMS to all agents with probability exceeding $(1-c^2/5)$, for any $c\in (0,1]$. For XOS valuations, stronger lower bounds hold: no randomized algorithm can ensure $c$-MMS to all agents with probability exceeding $(1-c/3)$, for any $c\in (0,1]$. Furthermore, no algorithm can achieve $\omega(1/\log \log n)$-MMS with any constant probability. All our lower bounds hold even for simple binary instances whose MMS values and MMS partitions can be computed in linear time.
item.dc:creator: Shuchi Chawla, Zhiyi Huang, Pooja Kulkarni, Ruta Mehta, Parnian Shahkar

item.title: A Tale of Two Walks: From Kac to KMP and Back
item.description: arXiv:2609.38044v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We reveal an unexpected connection between two interacting particle systems: Kac's walk and the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) process. We first establish a mixing-time analogue of Aldous's conjecture for the KMP process on general graphs: the mixing time of the $t$-particle process on any connected $d$-vertex graph is at most $O(\log d)$ times the corresponding single-particle mixing time, uniformly in $t$. As an application, we improve the mixing-time bound for coordinate hit-and-run on the $n$-dimensional standard simplex from $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ [KV26] to $O(n\log n)$, while removing the dependence on the initial distribution. We then show that the twirling channel induced by the parallel Kac's walk on the symmetric subspace can be exactly encoded by a Markov chain on partitions, which naturally lifts to a parallel KMP chain on the complete graph. We prove that $O(\log d+\log(1/\varepsilon))$ repetitions of the parallel Kac's walk suffice to approximate Haar twirling on the symmetric subspace of $(\mathbb{C}^d)^{\otimes t}$ to error $\varepsilon$, uniformly in all $t$. Our main technical contribution is a new structural property of KMP-type dynamics: conditional product structure, which holds for both the standard KMP processes on general graphs and the parallel KMP processes on complete graphs. Conditioned on suitable auxiliary randomness, the evolution of the labeled KMP process factorizes into independent single-particle updates. Combining this structure with an exact coupling, we remove the dependence on the number of particles from the mixing bounds for both unlabeled KMP models. This bypasses the $\log(\pi_{\min}^{-1})$ dependency from spectral-gap arguments, which is often prohibitively large for many-particle systems. Using this framework, we prove mixing bounds that are sharp up to logarithmic factors for both unlabeled KMP models.
item.dc:creator: Qian Chen, Jingcheng Liu, Minglong Qin, Leonard J. Schulman, Fang Song, Penghui Yao, Mingnan Zhao

item.title: Fast mixing of the SYK model at high temperatures
item.description: arXiv:2610.05953v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model is a strongly interacting fermionic system. Its dynamics are difficult to analyze with Lieb-Robinson bounds and cluster expansions due to its all-to-all disordered interactions. We prove that, with high probability over the disorder, the SYK model admits a quantum Gibbs sampler with a system-size-independent spectral gap at sufficiently high constant temperatures. This yields polynomial-time preparation of SYK Gibbs states on a quantum computer. While prior non-rigorous computations that suggested SYK thermalization were limited to studying local correlators, we emphasize that our result holds up to arbitrary inverse polynomial trace distance. Our proof introduces the pseudo-Lindbladian approach to fermions then applies two key new ideas: a Bochner inequality for quantum dynamics, and an especially simple SYK analysis based on a comparison to classical dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Yiyi Cai, Yongtao Zhan, Alexander Zlokapa

item.title: Large Growth Happens: Gaussian Elimination with Partial Pivoting on Random Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2610.08701v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove that the probability that Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting on $n \times n$ Gaussian random matrices has growth $\rho$ is at least inverse quasi-polynomial: $\Omega\left(\exp\left(-c \log^2 \left(\frac{\rho}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\log(n)\right)\right)$ for some constant $c > 0$. In particular, the probability of growth $\rho \ge n^{1/2 + \epsilon}$ is at least $\exp(- O (\epsilon^2 \log^3 (n) ))$. This lower bound breaks standard conjectures in the smoothed and average-case analysis of Gaussian elimination. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first non-trivial lower bound on the probability of large growth for Gaussian random matrices.
item.dc:creator: Daniel A. Spielman, Xifan Yu

item.title: A Sharp Dynamic Haussler Lemma
item.description: arXiv:2610.29898v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Haussler's covering lemma (JCTA 1995) gives the sharp $(C/\delta)^d$ metric-entropy bound for binary VC classes under normalized $\ell_1$ distance. We prove a sharp global dynamic analogue for bounded real-valued classes in normalized $\ell_p$, for every $1\le p<\infty$. Writing $d=\operatorname{sfat}_{\varepsilon/32}(\mathcal F)$, we obtain a global dynamic cover of size at most $(C/\varepsilon^p)^d$ for every horizon and $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Here a single family of deterministic causal experts, fixed independently of the instance sequence, covers every target on every sequence. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$, a matching worst-case lower bound $(c/\varepsilon)^{pd}$ holds already for binary classes on one fixed sequence, even with real-valued experts. The constants are universal, independent of $p$. For $p=2$, this resolves the horizon-independent sequential $\ell_2$ covering problem of Rakhlin, Sridharan, and Tewari (PTRF 2015) in a stronger global form. For $p=1$, it gives the sharp $(C/\delta)^{\operatorname{Ldim}(\mathcal H)}$ global dynamic covering bound for binary classes, resolving questions of Alon, Ben-Eliezer, Dagan, Moran, Naor, and Yogev (STOC 2021) and Malliaris and Moran (Trans. AMS 2024). Our proof combines rank-decreasing correction schedules and accurate sampled prefixes with exact continuations after target identification. Shared-parent routing distributes these continuations among eligible prefixes, eliminating the logarithmic overhead.
item.dc:creator: Shihao Shao, Dacheng Tao

item.title: Nearly-Optimal Time-Sample Trade-off in Consensus Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.40562v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How does the number of sampled opinions affect the time required to reach consensus in distributed consensus dynamics? We study the synchronous $h$-Majority, in which every node independently samples $h$ nodes uniformly at random with replacement in each round and adopts a most frequent sampled opinion, breaking ties uniformly at random. We show that $h$-Majority achieves the nearly-optimal trade-off between the sample size and the consensus time, among a broad class of consensus dynamics. In particular, we prove the following results. For every sample size $h \ge 3$ and for every initial configuration, we prove that the process reaches consensus with high probability within $$\widetilde{O}\left(1+\min\left\{\frac{1}{\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\}},\frac{\sqrt{n}}{h}\right\}\right)$$ rounds, where $n$ is the number of nodes and $p_{\max}$ is the largest initial fraction of nodes supporting any single opinion. This is the first bound on the consensus time for $h$-Majority that holds for every $h\ge3$ and every initial configuration. When the initially most popular opinion has a sufficiently large lead over every other opinion, we show that all nodes adopt this opinion with high probability within $O(\log n/\min\{h^2p_{\max},1\})$ rounds. We establish a matching lower bound up to polylogarithmic factors for any fixed update rule that treats all opinions symmetrically and that selects either a sampled opinion or the node's current opinion.
item.dc:creator: Francesco d'Amore, Joel Rybicki, Nobutaka Shimizu, Takeharu Shiraga, Robin Vacus

item.title: Constant-Factor Approximation for Capacitated Clustering in Low Dimension with $(1+\epsilon)k$ Centers
item.description: arXiv:2610.40625v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In many applications of $k$-median and $k$-means, including load balancing and redistricting, each center can serve only a bounded number of clients. This leads to capacitated clustering, in which a client may be forced to use a distant center because all nearby ones are full. This loss of locality defeats the techniques behind approximation schemes, and no constant-factor approximation is known in general metrics even for capacitated $k$-median. A long line of work therefore opens $K=k+\lfloor\epsilon k\rfloor$ centers for a fixed $\epsilon\in(0,1]$, while respecting the capacities exactly. We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for uniform soft capacities in low dimension, that is, when the clients or the center locations have bounded doubling dimension. With $K$ centers, its ratio is $3-2\epsilon$ for $k$-median and $9-8\epsilon$ for $k$-means, or $5-4\epsilon$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Apart from $k$-median in the plane, these are the first polynomial-time ratios bounded by a constant independent of $\epsilon$; previously, the best ratio was $O(\epsilon^{-2}\log(1/\epsilon))$, even for $k$-median. We also obtain ratios that stay bounded as $\epsilon\to0$ for non-uniform and hard capacities in low dimension, and ratios polylogarithmic in $1/\epsilon$ in general metrics. Our approach starts from a simple structural observation: a near-optimal uncapacitated solution can be split into fewer than $2k$ capacity-respecting blocks, so $2k$ centers already suffice, one per block. Our main tool, the rescue lemma, shows that once every block that sends clients to a center of the optimal solution is rescued (given a private center), that center can be closed, so each extra center effectively rescues about two blocks. This lets $\lfloor\epsilon k\rfloor$ extra centers rescue nearly an $\epsilon$-fraction of the blocks, yielding the linear dependence on $\epsilon$ in our ratios.
item.dc:creator: Kangke Cheng, Guanlin Mo, Hu Ding
